extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and scientists invited to review manuscripts for PLOS Medicine
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for researchers performing peer review for PLOS Medicine, including whether to accept invitations, how to assess manuscripts (validity, significance, methods, reporting), and standards for writing and submitting reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting an invitation to review
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept an invitation only if you have the knowledge, time and objectivity necessary to provide an unbiased assessment of the research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer invitations are sent by email from the Editorial Manager system. Use the links in the invitation email to accept or decline. In agreeing to complete a review, you also give permission to publish your review under a Creative Commons Attribution CC BY license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaring competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A competing interest is anything that interferes with or could be perceived as potentially interfering with, a thorough and objective assessment of a manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common examples: a recent or current collaboration with any of the authors; direct competition or a history of scientific conflict with any of the authors; an opportunity to profit financially from the work. Do not accept a review assignment if you have a competing interest or don’t feel able to give an objective assessment. If unsure, contact the journal office for advice. If asked to complete the review anyway, declare the competing interest when you submit your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crediting collaborators who helped with the review
rubrics_metrics.description: If you had help completing the review you must share your collaborator’s name with the journal via email.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful not to include your collaborator’s name in the text of the review itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep manuscripts and correspondence confidential and do not share information about submissions with anyone else unless previously agreed with the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are expected not to make use of any material or take advantage of any information they gain through the peer review process. Read the PLOS Confidentiality Policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling manuscripts you previously reviewed elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: If you reviewed the article at another journal, consider the manuscript as a new submission unless instructed otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind it may have been revised since the last evaluation and PLOS Medicine’s criteria for publication may differ. When you submit your review, let the editor know that you reviewed a previous version of the manuscript at another journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to complete your review within 8 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need more time to perform the review, email the journal as soon as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for publication — ethical and scientific validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts must be conducted in accordance with ethical standards and be scientifically valid to be eligible for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for publication — importance of the research question
rubrics_metrics.description: The research question is an important one to the community of researchers in this general area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for publication — substantial advance and clear implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The results provide a substantial advance over existing knowledge, with clear implications for patient care, public policy, or clinical research agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for publication — interest to clinicians and policymakers and Author Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Published together with an Author Summary written for general readers, the article is of interest to clinicians and policymakers who are not specialists in this topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the review
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the editors with an expert opinion regarding the validity and quality of the manuscript and supply authors with explicit feedback on how to improve their papers so they will be acceptable for publication in PLOS Medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify main claims and assess significance
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the main claims of the paper and how significant are they for the discipline?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claims are novel, important, and deserving of publication in the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualization within prior literature and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the claims properly placed in the context of the previous literature? Have the authors treated the literature fairly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for omitted key references, biased framing, or overclaiming relative to prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do the data and analyses fully support the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the presented data and analyses fully support the authors’ claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not, specify what other evidence or analyses are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods reporting and protocol deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether methods are reported in sufficient detail and whether any important deviations from provided protocols are explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PLOS encourages detailed methods as supporting information online. If a protocol is already provided (e.g., for an RCT), note any important deviations and whether explanations are adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether the paper is outstanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Is this paper outstanding in its discipline? If yes, what makes it outstanding? If not, why not?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide justification for claims of exceptional importance or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to relevant reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the study conforms to relevant guidelines such as CONSORT, MIAME, QUORUM, STROBE, and the Fort Lauderdale agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag missing checklist adherence or required reporting elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility — sufficient methodological detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Are details of the methodology sufficient to allow the experiments to be reproduced?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request additional procedural details, data, or analytic code if needed to reproduce results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Is any software created by the authors freely available?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage or request open access to software used to produce results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript organization and accessibility to non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the manuscript well organized and written clearly enough to be accessible to non-specialists?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PLOS Medicine expects clarity such that clinicians and policymakers who are not specialists can understand the work; recommend editorial or structural improvements where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directing comments to authors vs confidential comments to editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Although confidential comments to the editors are respected, any remarks that might help to strengthen the paper should be directed to the authors themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the confidential box only for matters you do not wish the authors to see (e.g., serious undisclosed competing interests or allegations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-review and evaluating revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are often asked to evaluate revised manuscripts and the authors’ response to reviewer comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make yourself available for re-review and questions from the editors when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reviewer report content and editorial editing
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS staff will not change reviewer comments intended for authors to read, except where language is inappropriate for professional communication or if comments contain confidential information or content that would pose a major risk if conveyed to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, staff will discuss wording changes with the reviewer before edits; if not feasible, minimal edits will be made. If concerns do not meet these criteria, staff or handling editors may advise authors that certain comments can be disregarded or clarify which comments do not need to be addressed. Once a decision has been delivered, PLOS will not edit or remove review reports, though staff may clarify which comments don't need addressing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting reviews — editorial resolution process
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers disagree fundamentally, editors may share all reviews with each reviewer and request additional comments to help reach a decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions are not necessarily by majority rule; editors evaluate reviewer recommendations alongside authors’ comments and other material; reviewers should know their recommendation is considered even if the final decision differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portability of reviews across PLOS journals
rubrics_metrics.description: If authors transfer their manuscript to another PLOS journal, your review will accompany it and you may be asked to re-review by editors at another PLOS journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers for any PLOS journal should be willing to have their reviews considered by the editors of another PLOS journal.
